item_name: Driverless Safety Concept and Required Documentation
competition_series: FSAE (SAE International, North America, uses the Driverless Systems Form/DSF); Formula Student Germany (FSG) and the FSG-family European series that share the Autonomous System Form/ASF and Electrical System Form/ESF review system (confirmed shared use by FS East 2022 rules)
summary: Every FSAE/FS driverless team must clear a stack of pre-competition safety deliverables before it is allowed to run: a Notice of Intent (NOI, ~7 months before a June event), a Driverless/Autonomous Systems Form (DSF/ASF) documenting 8 technical sections of the emergency-brake-system (EBS) architecture with ISO 26262/21448-style hazard reasoning, a Vehicle Status Video (VSV) proving the car drives under its own power, the Design Event submission, and passing the on-site EBS brake test and driverless technical inspection. These are reviewed asynchronously with automatic rejection/resubmission cycles (4 or 7 days to resubmit, escalating point penalties of 10 or 5 points per overdue day, +25/+50/+75 points for 3rd/4th/5th+ rejections, uncapped total penalty for the ASF) that consume real calendar time teams routinely underbudget. A single university-level ISO 26262 Concept Phase safety analysis (item definition, HARA, FSC, TSC) for the EBS alone was documented as a full one-semester (30-credit, ~5-6 month) master's thesis effort that still did not reach FMEA or Fault Tree Analysis, which the author explicitly deferred as future work - illustrating that the DSF's expectation of hazard-driven, traceable safety reasoning is a substantial, specialist-level workload, not a checkbox exercise. The most consequential downstream failure mode is not paperwork rejection but a safety-critical event exposed only at the dynamic EBS test itself, as shown by QUT Motorsport's December 2024 crash. Design judges (per the FSAE Driverless scoresheet) explicitly probe HARA/SOTIF understanding, fail-operational vs. fail-safe reasoning, and how the team verified its safety concept, meaning the documentation is not separable from the Design Event score.

year_by_year_timeline.year: T-9 to T-7 months (autumn before a June/July competition)
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Team formally declares intent to enter the Driverless class. FSAE 2026 NOI deadline was Nov 3, 2025 for the following June event, i.e. roughly 7 months lead time. Not committing does not bar a later change of mind, but not submitting bars later eligibility.

year_by_year_timeline.phase_name: Safety concept development (HARA / FSC / TSC-style reasoning)
year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: EBS mechanical architecture (accumulator sizing, redundant pneumatic/hydraulic circuits, deactivation valves) must be frozen enough to diagram
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Shutdown circuit, DSMS/LVMS switching, EBS relay and RSS bypass relay wiring must be finalized enough to schematic
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Continuous-monitoring and startup-check state machines (thresholds, failure reactions) must be defined in SI units for the flowcharts
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Internally, teams should be producing the equivalent of an ISO 26262 Concept Phase (item definition, HARA, Functional Safety Concept, Technical Safety Concept) referenced directly in the FSAE Design scoresheet's 'Functional Safety' judging criterion. A KTH master's thesis doing exactly this scope for the EBS alone (2018) took a full 30-credit (~1 semester, 5-6 month) academic project and still did not reach FMEA/FTA.

year_by_year_timeline.phase_name: DSF/ASF drafting, submission, and review rounds
year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Mechanical Assembly Drawings (DSF.7): renderings from multiple angles of every load-bearing DSB part, cut/transparent views of enclosed hydraulic assemblies, sealing-material call-outs
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Actuator Power Supply Schematic (DSF.2) and High Level Block Diagram (DSF.4): LV source, LVMS/DSMS, RSS bypass relay (with manufacturer/part number/contact certification), all DSB ECUs and watchdogs, full energy flow to the wheel brakes
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Continuous Monitoring Flowchart (DSF.3) and Startup Checks Flowchart (DSF.6), consistent component naming across every document (DSF.1.1.6), CAN DBC file (DSF.8) covering all DSB-monitored signals
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Submission of the 8-section DSF/ASF package (Overall formatting, Actuator Power Supply Schematic, Continuous Monitoring Flowchart, High Level Block Diagram, Pressure System Overview, Startup Checks Flowchart, Mechanical Assembly Drawings, CAN Database File/DBC). On FSG-family events sharing this review system, a rejection triggers an automatic 4-day (96h) or 7-day (168h) resubmission window depending on document type; missing either deadline costs 10 or 5 points per overdue day; the ASF specifically carries no cap on total penalty points, and a 3rd/4th/5th+ rejection adds a flat 25/50/75 points on top.

year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: TSAL/status-indicator visibility must be demonstrable on camera
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Team must submit video evidence of the completed vehicle driving under its own power (not towed/pushed), in required safety gear, before an Event-Website-specified deadline (historically early July for a late-July FSG event). Organizers' own guidance: 'Do not gamble with the upload deadline.' Late/failed VSV can gate on-site participation.

year_by_year_timeline.phase_name: Design Event report + on-site defense prep
year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Ties EBS/mechanical documentation into the Design judging 'Overall Vehicle Concept - Functional Safety' rubric (HARA per ISO 26262, foreseeable misuse/SOTIF per ISO 21448, fail-safe/fail-operational reasoning, safety validation evidence)
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Shutdown-system and redundancy narrative must match the submitted DSF exactly (DSF.1.1.6 naming consistency is explicitly checked)
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Team must be able to discuss uncertainty propagation from sensing to actuation, per the scoresheet's explicit note that judges probe 'the probabilistic nature of their system'
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Design judges (3-6 per team in First Round) score Overall Vehicle Concept (30 pts, includes Functional Safety), Software & Computation (30), Vehicle Performance (30), and Autonomous Functionality (60) against Design/Build/Refinement/Understanding criteria - the safety documentation directly feeds this 150-point sheet.

year_by_year_timeline.phase_name: Driverless technical inspection + EBS brake test
year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Physical DSB inspected against the Mechanical Assembly Drawings and Pressure System Overview submitted in the DSF
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Shutdown circuit, RSS integration, and EBS relay physically verified against the Actuator/Block Diagram; sensors/actuators are deliberately disconnected to test fault response
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Continuous monitoring and startup-check logic exercised live against the submitted flowcharts; Inspection Mission (sine-wave steering sweep, 25-30s) run with wheels off the ground
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Vehicle must pass Technical Inspection, Driverless Inspection, and the dynamic Emergency Brake System Test (accelerate to >=40 km/h within 20 m, remote-stop triggered, must stop within 8.5 m, average deceleration >10 m/s2, 200 ms max reaction time) before any dynamic event points are possible.

ramp_phases: Notice of Intent (~7 months out, low effort, administrative)
Safety-concept authoring: HARA/FSC/TSC-equivalent reasoning (typically starts 4-8 months out; a rigorous single-subsystem academic treatment of just this phase took ~1 semester for one engineer)

DSF/ASF 8-section documentation package drafting and internal review (typically 4-8 weeks of concentrated cross-disciplinary work: mechanical, electrical, and software leads must all contribute consistent, cross-referenced content)
DSF/ASF submission and resubmission cycles (each rejection costs 4-7 days minimum plus escalating point penalties; teams should budget at least 2 review rounds)
Vehicle Status Video production (requires a fully driving, safety-compliant car, so it is gated by hardware completion, not just paperwork - commonly a late crunch item)
Design Event report and defense prep (parallel track, due to the overlap between DSF content and the Functional Safety judging rubric)
On-site technical/driverless inspection and EBS brake test (the final, and highest-consequence, validation gate - see QUT Motorsport's Dec 2024 crash during exactly this test)
what_slipped: Across the FSG-family review system, rejections are the norm rather than the exception: the automatic 4/7-day resubmission clock plus escalating late-day penalties (10 or 5 pts/day) and per-rejection penalties (+25 at the 3rd rejection, +50 at the 4th, +75 at the 5th+) exist precisely because teams routinely fail to pass on the first submission - the ASF carries no cap on total penalty points, meaning a badly-managed document cycle can bleed an unbounded number of points before competition even starts. The KTH thesis data point shows that a rigorous, ISO 26262-conformant Concept Phase safety analysis for one subsystem (the EBS) is a multi-month specialist task on its own, and even then stopped short of FMEA/FTA - teams that treat the DSF as a form-filling exercise rather than budgeting real analysis time are the ones generating rejections. The single most damaging real-world slip found in this research is QUT Motorsport's Dec 2024 case: the team had a compliant, previously-passing EBS system on paper, but the live dynamic EBS test itself - the very last gate before competition - exposed a software/path-planning latency issue that the documentation and prior inspections had not caught, crashing the car and ending its competitive life for that season.
platform_prerequisites: The DSF's Actuator Power Supply Schematic and High Level Block Diagram cannot be finalized until the vehicle's core electrical architecture (LVMS/DSMS, shutdown circuit, RSS integration) is essentially frozen, meaning documentation work is gated by having a working, wired chassis, not just a design on paper. Practically this means a team needs its base EV platform (shutdown circuit, LV system) built and validated before the DSF package can be completed to a passing standard - documentation cannot get meaningfully ahead of hardware integration on the electrical side, only on the mechanical/pneumatic conceptual side.
ebs_design: The DSF explicitly requires teams to document (not merely build) 8 things about the DSB/EBS: (1) an Actuator Power Supply Schematic showing LV source, LVMS/DSMS, RSS bypass relay (with manufacturer, part number, and safety-contact certification), and actuator supply; (2) a Continuous Monitoring Flowchart with SI-unit thresholds and named watchdog handling; (3) a High Level Block Diagram showing the whole DSB including redundancy, all ECUs/watchdogs, full energy flow, and the EBS activation relay (named, with manufacturer/part number); (4) a Pressure System Overview naming every pneumatic/hydraulic component per EN 81346 with manufacturer/part number/max pressure, both redundant circuits shown separately, and PI-certified high-pressure tanks; (5) a Startup Checks Flowchart from DSMS-On to AS-Ready with independently-testable redundancy; (6) Mechanical Assembly Drawings of every load-bearing DSB part with multiple-view renderings and sealing-material call-outs; (7) a DBC CAN database file. Per DT.3.2.1, the EBS itself must be a passive, mechanically-energy-stored system (i.e., not solely motor-driven) directly supplied by GLVMS/DSMS/Remote-Stop-Relay/EBS-Relay with no delay - the dominant real-world implementation pattern across teams researched is a dual-redundant pneumatic accumulator (paintball-bottle-class tanks, ~8 bar working pressure typical per DSF example) actuating brake calipers through pneumatic cylinders/fluidic muscles, each circuit independently pressure-monitored and independently shut-off-capable.
ebs_development_duration: [uncertain] No team published an end-to-end 'EBS concept to passing brake test' duration figure. The closest proxy found: a full ISO 26262 Concept-Phase-only safety analysis (item definition, HARA, FSC, TSC) for an EBS, done as a dedicated 30-credit KTH master's thesis, took approximately one semester (~5-6 months, full-time equivalent for one engineer) and explicitly did not reach FMEA/FTA, which the author deferred as future work - implying that a genuinely rigorous safety case for the EBS alone, before any hardware validation, consumes months of specialist effort even before build/test begins.
ebs_cost_estimate: [uncertain] No consolidated EBS cost figure was found in sources reviewed for this documentation-focused deep dive; DSF example components (paintball-class air tanks, Festo pneumatic valves/cylinders, pressure regulators/sensors) are commodity industrial-pneumatics parts, suggesting a bill-of-materials in the low thousands of USD, but no team-published total was located. See the companion Testing Infrastructure research item for rig-cost context.
steering_actuation: N/A - not the focus of this documentation-centered item. Note only that the DSF requires the Actuator Power Supply Schematic to show the steering actuator's supply and switching path (DSF.2.1.1.d), and DT.2.2 requires the actuator to be mechanically decoupled/coupled between manual and autonomous modes, which must be demonstrable and consistently named across the DSF, Design Report, and physical inspection.
brake_actuation: N/A - out of scope for this item; see EBS design field above for the safety-critical DSB, which is the documentation-relevant braking system.
sensor_mounting_packaging: N/A - not a documentation-burden topic per se, though DI.1.2 requires teams to bring datasheets for all sensors, and documentation proving sensors meet local legislation, to Driverless Inspection.
compute_platform: N/A - not covered by the DSF, which is scoped to the Driverless System Brake (DSB) specifically, not the full autonomy compute stack.
sensor_suite: N/A - see sensor_mounting_packaging; the DSF's CAN DBC requirement (DSF.8) does require a documented signal set for whatever sensors feed the DSB/energy meter, with consistent naming across all submitted documents (DSF.1.1.6).
shutdown_circuit_implementation: The Shutdown Circuit (SDC) is the backbone the entire DSF documentation package is organized around: DT.4 requires a Driverless System Relay (normally-open, permissive), a Remote Stop Relay (in series with shutdown buttons, bypassed by a DSMS-supplied normally-closed relay with a certified forcibly-guided or mirrored contact in Manual Mode), and an Emergency Brake System Relay (fail-open, coil in parallel with the isolation relays) that starts EBS the instant the SDC opens. The Actuator Power Supply Schematic (DSF.2) and High Level Block Diagram (DSF.4) both must show this circuit explicitly (may be abbreviated 'SDC' in DSF.4 only), and the EBS relay must be individually named with manufacturer and part number (DSF.4.1.10) - this is one of the most heavily cross-checked items across DSF sections and technical inspection.
remote_stop_system: Standardized hardware supplied by Gross-Funk GmbH: a Control Box (sender) and Vehicle Module (receiver), SIL3/EN61508 and EMV certified, 25 mW signal strength, 12-24V supply, IP20 (receiver)/IP65 (sender), with a normally-open relay (max 4A) that must sit in the shutdown circuit and opens on shutdown, signal loss, or power loss. Uses CANopen (Node-ID 0x011, 500 kbps at competition) with a 200ms pre-alarm before a radio-loss-triggered shutdown. Teams needing North American frequencies require a separate E-Key; a distinct Race E-Key (returned immediately post-run) replaces the team's Training E-Key for scored dynamic runs, and teams may use the Race Key for EBS test runs only up until the first dynamic event opens.
status_indicators: The DSSI (Driverless System Status Indicator) must show Off/Ready(yellow continuous)/Driving(yellow flashing)/Finished(blue continuous)/Emergency(blue flashing), and a separate Driverless Mission Indicator (on the dash or near the DSMS) must clearly show the currently selected mission. Both are checked directly against DO.1.1.3/DO.1.4 at technical inspection and their behavior must match what is described in the DSF's monitoring/startup flowcharts.
custom_pcbs: N/A - not documented for this item; see individual team files for team-specific custom electronics.
software_stack: N/A - the DSF is scoped to hardware/mechanical/electrical documentation of the DSB, not the general autonomy software stack; see the Design Event scoresheet's separate 'Software & Computation' (30 pts) category for how software architecture, CI/CD, and testing rigor are judged independently of the DSF.
ci_cd_testing: N/A - not covered by the DSF; the Design scoresheet separately rewards CI/CD and HIL/regression testing rigor under Software Development Process.
data_logging: The DSF requires (DSF.8) a valid DBC file defining all DSB-monitored signals so officials can reproduce vehicle state after any EBS activation; per the Remote Stop System info sheet, EBS pressure signals (CAN-ID 0x500, 4x int16 channels) should be logged with at least one full redundant path represented if more than 4 signals are available, and all Driverless CAN signals must be little-endian with documented scaling. The FSAEOnline submission portal only accepts this subsection as a PDF, so teams commonly paste the raw DBC text into a word processor and export to PDF - a small but real formatting gotcha teams have had to work around.
open_source_repos: N/A - see individual team research items (e.g. QUT_Motorsport.json) for team-specific public repositories; none reviewed for this item publish their DSF/ASF submissions themselves (these are confidential to organizers).
critical_path_items: 1) The safety-concept authoring itself (HARA/FSC/TSC-equivalent reasoning) is a genuine specialist bottleneck, not a formality - the KTH thesis data point shows a single subsystem's Concept Phase alone is a multi-month task for one dedicated engineer, and most teams do not have a dedicated functional-safety engineer. 2) DSF/ASF review-round latency: each rejection costs a mandatory 4-7 day minimum resubmission window plus point penalties, so a team that submits late or with errors can lose 2-4+ weeks of calendar time to review cycles alone, compounding if cross-document naming (DSF.1.1.6) is inconsistent and triggers multiple rejections. 3) The dynamic EBS brake test at technical inspection is the true integration gate - it is where documentation, hardware, and software must all simultaneously prove correct under real dynamic conditions, and (per QUT Motorsport) is the single highest-consequence place for a previously 'compliant on paper' system to fail catastrophically.
long_lead_procurement: [uncertain] Not specifically documented for the safety/documentation deliverables themselves (these are labor-time, not procurement-gated). The one procurement item directly tied to safety compliance is the Remote Stop System (Gross-Funk Control Box + Vehicle Module, plus a North-America-specific E-Key where required) which teams must purchase from a single approved supplier; no public lead-time figure in weeks was found, but its single-source nature is a plausible schedule risk worth flagging for a new team.
testing_hours_before_first_comp: N/A - see companion research item 'Driverless Testing Infrastructure and Cadence' for this topic.
validation_strategy: The documentation stack IS a validation strategy in the rules' own design: DSF.3.2.1 explicitly instructs teams to 'derive test cases that may be used in technical inspection' directly from their Continuous Monitoring Flowchart, and DSF.6.2.1 does the same for the Startup Checks Flowchart - meaning a well-built DSF should double as the team's own internal fault-injection test plan. The FSG Beginners Guide explicitly recommends teams self-check every technical-inspection checklist item in advance (referencing prior years' inspection sheets) and design their EBS so it 'can perform multiple EBS tests in a row' or refill quickly, since technical inspection has limited time slots per team and a system that cannot be re-armed fast forces a costly requeue.
rules_compliance_challenges: The hardest single requirement to satisfy on paper and in practice is DT.3.2 EBS behavior under dynamic conditions (200 ms max reaction time, >10 m/s2 average deceleration, half-performance floor under single failure) combined with DSF.5.2.2's 'no single points of failure in a redundant system' requirement - satisfying this requires genuinely independent, cross-checked pressure paths (DSF.5.2.3 explicitly bans series-connected master cylinders/pressure transducers), which is easy to violate unintentionally. Cross-document naming consistency (DSF.1.1.6: identical component names across every submitted document) is a common, avoidable source of rejections. The RSS bypass relay's certification requirement (forcibly guided or mirrored safety contacts, DSF.2.1.5.c) requires teams to source and document a specific safety-rated relay, which is a compliance detail new teams commonly miss on a first pass.
tech_inspection_experience: Cross-team evidence (from companion team research) is mixed and instructive: QUT Motorsport passed all technical inspections on its first competition attempt (Dec 2022) yet still crashed during the EBS test two years later; UTFR (Univ. of Toronto) was reportedly the only team to pass all driverless inspections and run the autonomous autocross demonstration at FSAE Michigan 2025; Edinburgh (EUFS) did not pass scrutineering with its first self-built car (~2022) and only achieved a full combined pass piecewise over 2024-2025. The consistent pattern: passing DSF/ASF paper review does not guarantee passing physical technical inspection or the dynamic EBS test, and even teams with strong documentation histories can fail at the live gate.
ebs_test_experience: The DI.2 Emergency Brake System Test (2026 rules) requires the vehicle to accelerate in Driverless Mode to >=40 km/h within 20 m, then have Remote Stop triggered at a specific point, and come to a safe stop within 8.5 m (scalable if wet), performed in a straight line marked with cones similar to the Acceleration event, after other technical inspection is complete. This exact test is where QUT Motorsport's QEV-3D crashed in December 2024: a path-planning computation delay caused a sharp steering correction at 40 km/h just before the finish line, sending the car into a wall/tyre barrier; remote stop and EBS both activated but too late to prevent minor single-corner suspension damage, ending that car's competitive life. This demonstrates that a documented, previously-inspection-passing EBS/shutdown chain (correct per DSF/DT.4) is necessary but not sufficient - the live dynamic test exposes software-timing failure modes that static documentation review cannot catch.
documentation_burden: Substantial and commonly underestimated. Concretely dated data points found: (1) NOI due ~7 months before a June FSAE event (Nov 3 2025 for June 2026); (2) DSF/ASF is an 8-section technical package (Overall formatting + 7 content sections) requiring consistent terminology across every document, vector/300dpi graphics, and per-page team/document/page-number headers - explicitly designed to be checked mechanically as well as substantively; (3) on FSG-family events, rejections trigger automatic 4-day or 7-day resubmission clocks with 10 or 5 points/day late penalties and escalating +25/+50/+75-point rejection penalties (uncapped for the ASF), meaning a team that needs 2-3 review rounds (common, per the existence of an explicit 3rd/4th/5th-rejection penalty schedule) can lose multiple weeks and dozens of points before the car even leaves the shop; (4) the Vehicle Status Video requires a fully driving-under-its-own-power car and organizers explicitly warn teams not to leave it to the deadline; (5) underlying the DSF/ASF is an expectation of real ISO 26262/21448-style safety engineering (HARA, FSC, TSC, ideally FMEA/FTA) that a KTH master's thesis needed a full semester to partially complete for one subsystem. New teams should budget documentation as a parallel, resourced workstream starting 6-9 months out, not a 2-week task before the deadline.
autonomous_speeds_achieved: N/A - not this item's focus; the one directly relevant figure is the DI.2.2.2 EBS test's own required speed: >=40 km/h before Remote Stop is triggered.
ebs_deceleration_achieved: Rules requirement (not a measured team result): DT.3.2.5.b requires average deceleration >10 m/s2 under dry conditions (2026 rules), with DI.2.2.2 requiring the vehicle to stop within 8.5 m from >=40 km/h after Remote Stop triggers, and DT.3.2.5.a capping system reaction time at 200 ms. For historical context, an earlier (2018-era) KTH thesis cites an 8 m/s2 average-deceleration requirement from that year's rules, showing the performance bar has risen over time (8 -> >10 m/s2).
reliability_notes: QUT Motorsport's Dec 2024 EBS-test crash (see ebs_test_experience) is the standout reliability finding for this research item: a safety-critical live test exposed a latent software/path-planning-latency failure mode in a system whose documentation and prior inspections had been satisfactory. This is the clearest available evidence that FSAE/FSG's document-and-inspect gating process, while thorough, still leaves residual risk that only a real dynamic test surfaces - reinforcing why the rules mandate the EBS test as a distinct, final gate rather than relying on paper review alone.
top_mistakes: 1) Treating the DSF/ASF as a form to fill in near the deadline rather than the output of months of real hazard analysis - the KTH thesis shows even a narrow, single-subsystem ISO 26262 Concept Phase is a multi-month specialist task. 2) Inconsistent component naming across the DSF's 8 sections and the Design Report/physical vehicle (DSF.1.1.6 exists precisely because this is a common failure), which triggers avoidable rejections and costs 4-7+ days each time. 3) Assuming a documentation/inspection pass certifies real-world safety: QUT's car had passed technical inspection in prior years, yet its EBS-test crash in Dec 2024 shows that live dynamic conditions (specifically software timing under real sensor/planning latency) can defeat a system that looked correct on paper and in static inspection. 4) Underestimating single-source procurement risk on the standardized Remote Stop System (Gross-Funk hardware, plus a possible North-America-specific E-Key), which sits directly in the safety-critical shutdown circuit documented throughout the DSF.
advice_for_new_teams: From the rules and guides themselves: 'Do not gamble with the upload deadline. Teams on the waiting list will say thank you to you' (FSG, on the Vehicle Status Video). The FSG Beginners Guide explicitly recommends checking every technical-inspection checklist item in advance using prior years' inspection sheets, and designing the EBS so it 'should be able to perform multiple EBS tests in a row' or refill quickly, since inspection slots are time-limited and a slow-to-rearm EBS forces a costly requeue. The DSF's own System Requirements Checklists (one per section, e.g. DSF.3.2, DSF.4.2, DSF.5.2, DSF.6.2) are effectively a self-audit tool teams should run against their own design before submission, not just read after a rejection.
team_structure_dv: N/A - this item is a documentation/process deep-dive, not a team; however note that the DSF/ASF package spans mechanical (assembly drawings, pressure system), electrical (schematics, block diagrams, shutdown circuit), and software (monitoring/startup logic, CAN DBC) content simultaneously, meaning a team needs at least one contributor from each discipline actively involved in the DSF authoring process, not just one 'safety lead' working in isolation, to avoid the cross-document consistency failures that drive rejections.
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: [uncertain] No team-specific onboarding data was found for this documentation-focused item. Structurally, the DSF/ASF's requirement for consistent, cross-referenced technical writing over months (not a one-off event) makes it a natural single-point-of-failure risk if only one student 'owns' the safety documentation and graduates/departs before knowledge is captured - new teams should treat DSF authorship as a role with a written internal template and a named successor, given how much of the review-cycle penalty structure rewards getting it right early rather than iterating live against the clock.
budget_estimate: N/A - this item is a process/documentation deep-dive, not a cost analysis; no consolidated dollar figure for 'documentation cost' exists since the burden is primarily person-hours, not procurement. See ebs_cost_estimate for the one adjacent hardware cost note.
recommended_sequence: 1) At program kickoff, assign a cross-disciplinary safety-documentation owner (not just one engineer) and start HARA-style hazard identification in parallel with early mechanical/electrical architecture decisions, budgeting months, not weeks, given the KTH thesis precedent. 2) Freeze the shutdown circuit and DSB electrical architecture early, since the DSF's core diagrams (Actuator Power Supply Schematic, High Level Block Diagram) cannot be finalized until this is stable. 3) Draft the DSF/ASF's 8 sections in parallel with hardware build (not after), running each section's own System Requirements Checklist as a self-audit before first submission, to minimize costly rejection cycles. 4) Submit NOI and begin DSF drafting the moment the season opens (~9 months out), targeting DSF submission with enough buffer (6+ weeks) to absorb 1-2 rejection/resubmission cycles without touching the competition deadline. 5) Once hardware is built, stage the EBS validation (see companion Testing Infrastructure item) well before the on-site EBS test, since that live test - not the paperwork - is the true final safety gate, as QUT Motorsport's 2024 crash demonstrates. 6) Rehearse the physical technical-inspection checklist internally in advance using prior years' published inspection sheets.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: Highly applicable. A team with a running EV and ~9 software-focused members over a 24-month window (June 2026-June 2028) should treat safety documentation as a first-class workstream from month 1, not a pre-competition scramble: assign a named DSF/ASF owner early, budget real calendar time (months, not a sprint) for HARA/FSC/TSC-style reasoning informed by the KTH thesis precedent, and build the DSF's diagrams incrementally as the electrical/mechanical architecture stabilizes rather than reverse-engineering them from a finished car at the deadline. Given the team is software-heavy, extra discipline is needed to ensure the mechanical/electrical DSF content (assembly drawings, pressure system, block diagrams) gets equal, early attention rather than being left until last - and the team should explicitly plan and rehearse the live EBS test as a distinct, high-risk validation event (see companion Testing Infrastructure item), since QUT Motorsport's case shows that passing paperwork and prior inspections does not guarantee surviving that specific test.
